## LLM Recipe

### 1.3 Pretraining &amp; Optimization

#### [Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17876>)

The updated Muon study adds norm-reset interventions and 3.4B-parameter runs to an earlier investigation of temporary weight decay. Swapping weight norms at the end of decay transfers much of the later loss benefit in the tested small models, while larger-model experiments show why early loss regressions should be assessed again at the final training budget. These controls strengthen a specific optimization diagnosis, rather than establishing a universal decay schedule.

### 1.8 Distillation &amp; Model Compression

#### [Folding Language Models into Themselves](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18113>)

New controlled experiments evaluate Concertina, which compresses a pretrained model by repeatedly applying shared blocks with token-dependent low-rank corrections initialized from adjacent teacher layers. The study separates folding topology, token gating and training-data coverage, showing how a smaller stored model can recover much of a teacher's tested capability through distillation. Parameter savings retain the original computation depth and key-value cache, so they do not establish faster inference.

#### [CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17808>)

CarryOn separates a compact execution-state note from source-linked evidence fragments, using a trained 0.6B selector to recover older records without separate LLM context-management calls. Across three benchmarks and three Actors, it reports 75.7% equally weighted task success, 6.7 percentage points above the strongest overall baseline, offering a practical way to retain exact details during long workflows. These are single-run results with a separate selector per benchmark; the reported resource metrics exclude local selector and pruning compute and do not establish end-to-end savings.

## AI Training &amp; Inference Infra

### 3.2 RL &amp; Rollout Infrastructure

#### [TIDE: Reclaiming Lost Performance In On-Policy Reinforcement Learning](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17924>)

TIDE repurposes GPUs from completed or consolidated rollouts for gradient computation, while delaying the optimizer update until the entire synchronous on-policy batch is finished. Overlapping training with the rollout tail and migrating requests to improve decode batching gives reported 1.16–1.36× end-to-end speedups across two tasks on three single-node GPU testbeds. This offers a way to recover idle capacity without introducing stale-policy rollouts, although multi-node behavior and downstream training-quality equivalence were not established.

### 3.3 Inference Engines &amp; Serving

#### [Superfluid: New Local and Heterogeneous-Fleet Evaluation of an Existing LLM Server](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17753>)

A new study of the existing Superfluid server evaluates priority scheduling, cached-prefix reuse and whole-session placement across local machines that each hold a complete model replica. In a six-device heterogeneous fleet, all 5,041 requests complete as nodes join and one is killed, while output throughput rises from 112 to 534 tokens per second. It provides a practical reference for resilient local agent serving, although fleet placement lacks a controlled baseline and model sharding is unsupported.

### 3.4 Attention, KV Cache &amp; Memory Systems

#### [Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18459>)

Callo drafts tokens using a cache invalidated by an agent’s context edits while a separate prefill GPU recomputes exact state, then verifies every committed token against the repaired cache. This turns part of a cache-miss wait into useful generation, yielding reported 1.05–1.19× mean request-latency speedups in moderate-load, two-H200 session replays. Benefits require reusable session state and spare decode capacity; larger deployments were evaluated through simulation.
